I wrote the pitch below, but I left out "proven hit." For a game that hasn't been published yet, with 23 ratings, backers will read that as hype, and some will check. What you can actually prove is stronger: 140 playtests, an 8.1 rating, and 1,240 people waiting for launch. The pitch puts those numbers up front and says plainly what they are.

<final_document>
**The light has to burn every night. Can your family last until spring?**

On a rocky stretch of coast, a lighthouse keeper's family faces the longest season of the year. Storms roll in. Supplies run low. And every night, no matter what, the lamp at the top of the tower has to be lit. Ships are counting on it, and so is everyone inside.

**[GAME TITLE]** is a cooperative board game for 1 to 4 players. You don't play against each other. You win or lose together as one family. Each day you decide who tends the light, who keeps the household going, and what you can afford to give up before the thaw.

**Built at the table**

This game wasn't designed in one burst of inspiration. It came from three years of watching people play it.

Since 2023, I've run **140 playtest sessions with about 60 different players**: families, longtime hobby gamers, and people who had never tried a cooperative game. Nearly every session changed something. Rules got cut, choices got harder, and the tension got sharper. What's left is the version that kept people around the table saying "one more winter."

I took it to **two conventions**, and the **23 players who have rated it on BoardGameGeek give it an average of 8.1**. And **1,240 of you** signed up to hear the moment this campaign went live. That's why we're here today. Thank you.

**Who's making this**

I'm not a big publisher. By day I'm a land surveyor, and this is my first game and my first campaign. I won't pretend otherwise.

Surveying turns out to be good training for this. You measure twice, you check your numbers against the real world, and you don't sign off on anything you can't stand behind. I've tried to run this campaign the same way.

**Where your pledge goes**

Our goal is **$28,000**, and that number comes from real quotes, not guesses:

- **Manufacturing:** The factory has quoted $17,400 to produce 1,500 copies.
- **Shipping:** Getting a copy to your door in the US costs about $9, and that's **included in your $49 pledge**.
- **The rest** covers platform and payment fees and a buffer for the surprises every first-time creator gets warned about.

I'll post updates at every stage, including factory proofs, production photos, and shipping progress, so you always know where your copy is. If something goes wrong, you'll hear it from me first.

**Why back now**

Backing on day one gets you the game at the campaign price, and it gets a first-time designer's project funded early. Early funding is what turns a campaign into a real print run.

If you've ever wanted a cooperative game that feels less like solving a puzzle and more like holding something together with people you care about, this is it.

**Help us keep the light on.**

**[Back the project]**
</document>

- **Check the ratings site.** I assumed "the main board game ratings site" means BoardGameGeek. Change the name if it's a different site.
- **Check the budget.** At $49, your $28,000 goal is about 572 backers. That works out to roughly $5,100 in shipping plus about $2,500 to $2,800 in platform and payment fees. Add the $17,400 factory quote and very little is left for art, tariffs, freight from the factory, fulfillment, or extra copies. Check that before launch, because a budget that's too tight is the most common way first campaigns get into trouble. The pitch also doesn't say what happens to the roughly 900 extra copies; one sentence on that (retail, conventions, or late pledges) would help.

How I got the budget figures: $28,000 at $49 is about 572 backers. Shipping for 572 copies is about $5,100, and 10% fees on $28,000 is $2,800. Add the $17,400 factory quote and you've spent about $25,300, which leaves roughly $2,600.

That $2,600 has to cover a few costs that aren't in your numbers yet:

- **Freight from the factory to your fulfillment center.** This is often several thousand dollars on its own.
- **Tariffs or import duties**, if the game is printed overseas.
- **Fulfillment or warehouse fees**, unless you're packing and mailing every box yourself.

If any of these turn out to be large, raise the goal before launch. Running short after the campaign is much harder to fix. Once you have those quotes, I can update the budget section.
